title: Jeffries Easily Wins Caucus Vote to Be Next Speaker of the House
author: Nik Popli
body:
House Democrats nominated Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York for Speaker on Wednesday, putting him one step closer to becoming the first Black American to lead the chamber after steering his party to a sweeping victory in this month's midterm elections.

Jeffries, 56, faced no challenger in the closed-door election and secured the nomination in a 251 to 11 vote. The ballots were cast secretly through an application on lawmakers' phones, leaving the identities of those who opposed him undisclosed unless they chose to make their votes public.

The vote marked a milestone in Jeffries's political career, four years after he succeeded Nancy Pelosi as the top House Democrat and more than a decade after he entered Congress. Now, he is preparing to take charge of a chamber where Democrats are projected to hold 259 seats, a commanding majority that would give him considerably more room to maneuver than the narrow Republican majority that preceded it.

Immediately after the vote, seven incoming progressive Democrats confirmed they had voted against Jeffries, including Representatives-elect Claire Valdez of New York, Darializa Avila Chevalier of New York, Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, Melat Kiros of Colorado, Donavan McKinney of Michigan, and Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania. (Representative-Elect Frederick Haynes of Texas was also on the list, but did not make it to the vote because he woke up feeling unwell, his office said.) They said in a joint statement that they had been negotiating with Jeffries over the party’s agenda and had made progress, but were not yet satisfied with the commitments they had received.

"Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” the lawmakers said. "While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership. Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no."

The defections did little to dismiss what was an otherwise decisive show of support for Jeffries, whose nomination was put forward by Representatives Teresa Leger Fernández of New Mexico, Mark Pocan of Wisconsin, Derek Tran of California, Rebecca Bennett of New Jersey, and Jim Clyburn of South Carolina. He will serve alongside Representatives Ted Lieu of California as Democratic caucus chair, Katherine Clark of Massachusetts as majority leader, and Pete Aguilar of California as majority whip. The full House will vote to formally elect its leaders when the new Congress convenes on Jan. 3.

The transition from minority leader to Speaker will put Jeffries at the center of the political battles during the final two years of President Trump's term, giving Democrats control over the House's legislative agenda and investigative committees. His party has promised to use that authority to scrutinize the Trump Administration and demonstrate to voters that Democrats can govern ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

“Our message to the American people who are struggling in this failed economy is a simple one,” Jeffries said at a news conference following the leadership vote. “We hear you, we see you, we feel you, and House Democrats are committed to making life better for you.”

Wednesday's vote was conducted by secret ballot, a decision Jeffries announced Tuesday after some of his allies had favored nominating him by acclamation, without a formal tally. The recorded vote was intended to allow lawmakers to register their views privately, with the results revealing the level of support for Jeffries but not how individual members voted.

For some of the party's most senior members, the proceedings were an occasion to reflect on the historical significance of Jeffries's ascent. "This is a very surreal moment for me," Clyburn, a longtime South Carolina Democrat and former member of the House leadership, told reporters before entering the room. "And when it comes my turn to second his nomination, I'm going to be thinking about John, Lillian, and Emily,” he said, referring to the late John Lewis, an influential civil rights activist and congressman.

Representative Steny Hoyer of Maryland, who served for years alongside Pelosi and Clyburn in the party's previous leadership team, recalled witnessing the election of the first woman to become speaker. "It's a historic time," Hoyer said as he entered the room. "I've now served here for the first woman who was elected speaker of the House, and now we're going to see the first African American. I think it's a testimony to the progress that we've made in America."

Pushback from progressives

The nomination followed an extensive effort by Jeffries and his allies to consolidate support in the days since the election. They solicited endorsements from major Democratic factions, contacted lawmakers who had expressed reservations and sought to meet with members of the large incoming class before Wednesday's vote. Jeffries personally met with leaders of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, the New Democrat Coalition, and the Blue Dog Coalition.

The push came amid a campaign by progressive activists to persuade Democrats to reject Jeffries, whom some critics regard as too closely aligned with corporate interests and insufficiently willing to challenge the party's establishment. Congressional offices were inundated with calls and emails, and an online petition seeking an alternative candidate attracted more than a million signatures.

At a Democratic conference in Denver over the weekend, protesters repeatedly interrupted Jeffries with demands for Medicare for All, a Green New Deal, and an embargo on American weapons transfers to Israel. Some protesters also gathered Wednesday outside the room where Democrats were voting on leadership.

Progressive lawmakers have pressed Jeffries to promise a committee markup next year on Medicare for All legislation and bring forward the Block the Bombs Act, which would restrict certain offensive weapons transfers to Israel.

Asked on Wednesday if he would move towards the progressive left on these issues, Jeffries declined to commit. “We're going to work together to find the highest common denominator in order to make life better for the American people,” he said.

The public pressure from progressives did not translate into an organized challenge inside the House Democratic caucus as it did in the upper chamber, where Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has launched a bid to replace Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the current Democratic leader, over similar frustrations with the party's leadership. Though Schumer appears likely to retain his leadership post, Senate Democrats aren’t expected to settle that contest until next month.

In the House, prominent Democrats whose names circulated as possible alternatives to Jeffries declined to run. Representative Jamie Raskin of Maryland ruled out a bid as he’s in line to chair the powerful House Judiciary Committee, while Representative Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts, the subject of an online effort to draft her, made clear that she did not want the position. "I do not need to be the speaker of the House to speak for the people," Pressley told constituents at a town hall on Monday.

Jeffries’ path to the gavel

Minutes after his selection as the Speaker-designate, Jeffries posted a childhood photograph of himself on social media and quoted his favorite rapper, the Notorious B.I.G. “Stay far from timid, only make moves when your heart’s in it and live the phrase Sky’s the Limit,” the caption read.

Now on the doorstep of history, Jeffries reflected on how far he had come from his upbringing in Brooklyn, where he grew up as the son of an Air Force veteran and a social worker. “I was raised in a working-class neighborhood in Crown Heights,” he said at Wednesday’s news conference. “During the first 12 years of my life, my congresswoman—though I never met her—was Shirley Chisholm, a trailblazer extraordinaire. And part of the journey that all of us are on is that we recognize we stand on the shoulders of so many giants, and that young man was someone who was being so effectively represented by Shirley Chisholm, and now he has an opportunity…to try to do the same for the children of America for such a time as this.”

Jeffries often recalls how the devastation of the crack epidemic during the 1980s shaped his interest in public service and his desire to improve conditions for working-class families who remained in struggling neighborhoods. After attending the State University of New York at Binghamton, Georgetown University and New York University School of Law, Jeffries worked as a corporate lawyer before turning to politics. He lost his first two campaigns for the New York State Assembly, but he eventually won a seat in the Legislature. In 2012, he challenged a longtime Democratic congressman who withdrew from the race, clearing a path for his election to the House.

In Congress, Jeffries has developed a reputation as a disciplined political communicator and coalition builder, cultivating relationships across the party's ideological spectrum as he rose through its leadership ranks. When Pelosi stepped aside after the 2022 elections, he succeeded her as the top House Democrat, becoming the first Black lawmaker to lead either party in Congress.

Representative Steven Horsford of Nevada, the former chair of the Congressional Black Caucus and a close friend of Jeffries, called him a “consensus builder” and "listener.”

“I came in with Speaker-to-be Jeffries as a freshman,” Horsford said. “He's about building coalition. Yes, we're a diverse party. We have different viewpoints, but in the end, we're here for one common goal, and that is to deliver for the American people.”

Representative Troy Carter of Louisiana, who is also Black, credited Jeffries for the party's resounding wins in the midterms. "It was his strategy to pick good candidates, to fund good candidates, to give us the ability to reform our government the way the American people spoke clearly," Carter said. "Hakeem Jeffries has been the architect of that."

Jeffries' election as speaker would carry a historic significance beyond his own career, placing a Black American for the first time in an office second in the line of presidential succession, after the Vice President. It would also come more than 150 years after Joseph Rainey of South Carolina became the first Black member of the House during Reconstruction.

“America is a great country, but not a perfect country,” Jeffries said Wednesday. “But the framers of this democracy gave every generation the ability to work hard, to show up, to speak up, stand up, and help the country march toward a more perfect union. And that's what House Democrats at this moment represent: people from all walks of life, different corners of the country, who are here in order to make a difference in the lives of the American people.”

Debate over working with Republicans

Democrats have promised to use their control of Congress to pursue an ambitious legislative agenda and subject the Trump Administration to the kind of scrutiny that Republican leaders have largely resisted. The House's investigative committees would be able to examine allegations of corruption and abuses of executive authority, as well as the administration's handling of the war in Iran. Some Democrats are openly discussing impeachment proceedings against senior administration officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

But their ability to enact legislation will remain constrained by Trump's veto power and the Senate's 60-vote threshold for advancing most bills. Those obstacles have helped fuel a debate over whether the party should concentrate on legislation that might attract Republican support or pursue more ambitious measures that could establish its priorities for the 2028 election.

Jeffries has sought to leave room for both approaches, outlining an agenda organized around affordability and accountability. His immediate priorities include restoring enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits that expired earlier this year, reversing Republican Medicaid spending cuts, and repealing tariffs imposed by the Trump Administration.

Less than 24 hours before the nomination vote, Jeffries held a news conference and laid out more of his legislative vision. He embraced proposals to lower the Medicare eligibility age, expand coverage to include dental, vision and hearing benefits, and guarantee health coverage for children. "Those are bold actions, meaningful actions, important actions that can be taken on our march toward universal health coverage," Jeffries told reporters.

The proposals drew praise from Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, the leading proponent of Medicare for All, who said they resembled the first stage of his plan to move the country toward a single-payer system. But Jeffries has stopped short of endorsing Medicare for All itself, a distinction that illustrates the policy disagreements he will encounter even on an issue that Democrats have identified as a central priority.

The Congressional Progressive Caucus is expected to grow to more than 100 members in the next Congress, while the New Democrat Coalition, the largest ideological faction in the House Democratic Caucus, will number more than 140. Both groups support expanding access to health care and reversing Republican cuts, but they differ over whether Democrats should seek to replace the existing insurance system. The New Democrats have expressed skepticism about Medicare for All, arguing that competition among private insurers can help control costs.

Progressives are also seeking more aggressive action on corporate power, campaign finance, and American military assistance to Israel, among other issues. Their growing ranks could give them substantial influence over the House agenda, even if their efforts to challenge Jeffries's leadership gained little traction.

The political circumstances are almost the reverse of those confronting Pelosi when Democrats last reclaimed the House during a Trump presidency. In 2018, it was moderate Democrats who objected to her return as speaker, arguing that the party needed new leadership after years under her command. Pelosi ultimately overcame the resistance and went on to wield considerable authority over Trump's first term, overseeing major investigations and two impeachments of the President. Jeffries now faces skepticism primarily from the left, though he approaches the speakership with a larger majority and without the organized challenge that confronted his predecessor.

Representative-elect Don Leonard of Ohio said in a video posted to social media last week that senior Democrats had warned him they would make his life a "living hell" if he refused to support Jeffries. Leonard posted a picture of his ballot on Wednesday afternoon, showing that he was one of the 11 Democrats voting against Jeffries.

Still, Jeffries's allies dismissed suggestions that the dissent could substantially weaken his authority. "Given the size of our majority that we won by, you know, I don't think any of the pressures some people think he's going to face are going to be an issue," Representative Josh Gottheimer of New Jersey, a centrist Democrat, told reporters Wednesday.

Asked if he feels the need to negotiate with the 11 lawmakers who defected, Jeffries responded bluntly: “The results of today's election speak for themselves. We're going to work hard throughout every corner of the caucus to deliver for the American people. Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other.”

Hakeem Jeffries Easily Wins Caucus Vote to Be Next U.S. Speaker of the House
